Getting started with PP

Manuel Reif

Source: vignettes/intro_pp.Rmd
intro_pp.Rmd

PP estimates person parameters (abilities) when the item parameters are already known, for example from an earlier calibration or an item bank. It is the right package if

  1. you have item responses of a group of persons,
  2. you have item parameters for these items, which are treated as fixed,
  3. the items follow the 1PL to 4PL model, the (generalized) partial credit model, or a mix of both,

and you want ability estimates (MLE, WLE, MAP, EAP or a robust estimate), jackknife estimates, plausible values or person fit statistics.

This vignette shows the estimation functions. Person fit is the topic of vignette("intro_pfit"). Estimation and person fit in one step and models fitted with the eRm package are shown in vignette("ppass_erm").

A 3PL test

The data set fourpl_df contains the responses of 60 persons to 12 items, together with an id and the sex of each person. The item parameters are attributes of the data set.

library(PP)
data(fourpl_df)
head(fourpl_df[, 1:7])
#>        id sex Item1 Item2 Item3 Item4 Item5
#> 1 LVL0694   w     1     1     1     1     0
#> 2 BBU1225   w     1     1     1     1     1
#> 3 MJN2028   w     1     1     1     1     1
#> 4 TSU0771   m     1     1     1     0     1
#> 5 XDS0698   w     1     1    NA     1     1
#> 6 BOS1292   w     0     0     0     0     0

diff_par  <- attr(fourpl_df, "diffpar")
slope_par <- attr(fourpl_df, "slopes")
low_par   <- attr(fourpl_df, "lowerA")
items <- as.matrix(fourpl_df[, -(1:2)])

PP_4pl() covers all dichotomous models. Which model is used depends on the item parameters you supply: difficulties (thres) alone give the 1PL model, adding slopes gives the 2PL model, adding lowerA gives the 3PL model, and adding upperA as well gives the 4PL model. Here the difficulties, slopes and lower asymptotes are known, so the 3PL model is used.

res_mle <- PP_4pl(respm = items, thres = diff_par, slopes = slope_par, lowerA = low_par,
                  type = "mle")
#> Warning: 1 person(s) without a solution inside 'range' = c(-6, 6): the estimate
#> is set to the bound (status "boundary" in $estimates).
head(res_mle$estimates, 8)
#>     estimate        SE nsteps  status
#> 1 -0.9056597 0.7679868      4      ok
#> 2  1.8450588 1.0216306      4      ok
#> 3  1.0924751 0.9980509      4      ok
#> 4  1.3535510 1.0147741      5      ok
#> 5  0.3943829 0.9449658      4      ok
#> 6       -Inf        NA      0 extreme
#> 7  2.6716349 1.0175032      4      ok
#> 8  1.3617838 1.0151357      5      ok

The result is a list. Its main part is the data.frame $estimates with one row per person, in the order of the response matrix:

  • estimate and SE: the ability estimate and its standard error,
  • nsteps: the number of Newton steps needed for this person,
  • status: "ok" if the estimate converged inside range (default c(-6, 6)); "extreme" for persons with all answers right or wrong, who have no finite maximum likelihood estimate; "boundary" if there is no solution inside range and the estimate is set to its limit; "no_response" for persons without any answer; "not_converged" if the estimation did not converge within maxsteps steps.
summary(res_mle, nrowmax = 5)
#> PP Version: 0.7.0 
#> 
#> Call: PP_4pl(respm = items, thres = diff_par, slopes = slope_par, lowerA = low_par,      type = "mle") 
#> - job started @ Mon Oct 12 12:26:50 2026 
#> 
#> Estimation type: mle 
#> 
#> Status of the persons:
#> 
#>            ok       extreme      boundary   no_response not_converged 
#>            57             2             1             0             0 
#> 
#> Newton steps: at most 6 
#> -------------------------------------
#>   estimate     SE nsteps status
#> 1  -0.9057 0.7680      4     ok
#> 2   1.8451 1.0216      4     ok
#> 3   1.0925 0.9981      4     ok
#> 4   1.3536 1.0148      5     ok
#> 5   0.3944 0.9450      4     ok
#> --------> output truncated <--------

Person 35 answered only item 8 correctly, the item with the highest guessing parameter, and all easier items wrong (item 7 is missing). Under the 3PL model the likelihood of this pattern keeps rising as the ability decreases, so there is no maximum inside range. The estimate is set to the lower limit, the status is "boundary", and PP_4pl() gives a warning.

coef() returns the estimates as a vector and as.data.frame() the table, so the estimates can easily be added to the person data:

dat <- data.frame(fourpl_df[, 1:2], as.data.frame(res_mle)[, c("estimate", "SE")])
head(dat)
#>        id sex   estimate        SE
#> 1 LVL0694   w -0.9056597 0.7679868
#> 2 BBU1225   w  1.8450588 1.0216306
#> 3 MJN2028   w  1.0924751 0.9980509
#> 4 TSU0771   m  1.3535510 1.0147741
#> 5 XDS0698   w  0.3943829 0.9449658
#> 6 BOS1292   w       -Inf        NA

Missing responses (NA) are allowed; the ability of a person is estimated from the items they answered.

Choosing the estimation type

type selects the estimator:

  • "mle": maximum likelihood. Persons with all answers in the lowest or highest category get -Inf/Inf.
  • "wle" (default): weighted likelihood (Warm, 1989). It is less biased than the MLE and finite for extreme scores.
  • "map" and "eap": maximum and mean of the posterior with a normal prior N(mu, sigma2) (default N(0, 1)). The prior may differ between persons. The EAP is computed on a grid of ability values; its SE is the posterior standard deviation.
  • "robust": a Huber-type estimator (Schuster & Yuan, 2011), which downweights unexpected answers to items far from the person’s ability.
res_wle <- PP_4pl(respm = items, thres = diff_par, slopes = slope_par, lowerA = low_par)
res_eap <- PP_4pl(respm = items, thres = diff_par, slopes = slope_par, lowerA = low_par,
                  type = "eap", mu = ifelse(fourpl_df$sex == "w", 0.2, -0.2), sigma2 = 0.8)
head(cbind(mle = coef(res_mle), wle = coef(res_wle), eap = coef(res_eap)))
#>             mle        wle        eap
#> [1,] -0.9056597 -0.9363878 -0.4314707
#> [2,]  1.8450588  1.8106689  0.9679416
#> [3,]  1.0924751  0.9690544  0.6513154
#> [4,]  1.3535510  1.2235755  0.4553555
#> [5,]  0.3943829  0.2518466  0.3179423
#> [6,]       -Inf -4.7299643 -2.0455811

Polytomous and mixed tests

PP_gpcm() estimates abilities for the generalized partial credit model. With all slopes equal to 1 (the default) this is the partial credit model. thres has one column per item with its thresholds; items with fewer categories have NA below their last threshold. A first row of zeros is optional.

thres <- rbind(c(-1.5, -1, -0.5, 0, 0.5),
               c(0, 0.5, 1, 1.2, NA),
               c(1, 1.5, NA, 2, NA))
slopes <- c(1, 1.2, 0.8, 1.1, 0.9)
set.seed(1234)
x_gpcm <- sim_gpcm(thres = thres, alpha = slopes, theta = rnorm(200))
res_gpcm <- PP_gpcm(respm = x_gpcm, thres = thres, slopes = slopes, type = "wle")
head(res_gpcm$estimates)
#>      estimate        SE nsteps status
#> 1 -1.30077829 0.7936594      4     ok
#> 2 -0.09948067 0.6185704      4     ok
#> 3  1.87419642 0.6987634      3     ok
#> 4 -3.08511969 1.5519539      4     ok
#> 5  0.83380576 0.5892473      4     ok
#> 6 -0.74101448 0.6909744      4     ok

For a test with dichotomous and polytomous items, use PPall(). Each column of thres holds the thresholds of one item: a 4PL item has a single threshold (its difficulty), a GPCM item has several. findmodel() tells the two apart and is the default for model2est. Lower and upper asymptotes apply to the 4PL items only.

thres_mix <- rbind(c(-1, 0, 1, -0.5, 0.3),
                   c(NA, NA, NA, 0.6, 1.1))
findmodel(thres_mix)
#> [1] "4PL"  "4PL"  "4PL"  "GPCM" "GPCM"
x_mix <- sim_mixed(thres = thres_mix, alpha = c(1, 1.3, 0.9, 1, 1),
                   lowerA = c(0.2, 0.1, 0.15, 0, 0), theta = rnorm(200))
res_mix <- PPall(respm = x_mix, thres = thres_mix, slopes = c(1, 1.3, 0.9, 1, 1),
                 lowerA = c(0.2, 0.1, 0.15, 0, 0), type = "map")
summary(res_mix$estimates$estimate)
#>       Min.    1st Qu.     Median       Mean    3rd Qu.       Max. 
#> -1.3044946 -0.4941779 -0.0471063  0.0009135  0.5158184  1.4540105

sim_4pl(), sim_gpcm() and sim_mixed() simulate responses for given item and person parameters, as used above.

Jackknife

JKpp() leaves out each answered item once, estimates the ability again and combines the pseudovalues into a jackknife estimate and standard error (Wainer & Wright, 1980). cmeth = "median" and cmeth = "AMT" (Andrews’ sine estimator) give robust estimates; the standard error is the same for all three.

jk <- JKpp(res_wle)
head(jk$estimates)
#>     estimate        SE  L excluded status
#> 1 -0.9723726 0.6735435 12        0     ok
#> 2  1.8740917 0.6208916 12        0     ok
#> 3  1.0570466 0.4916653 12        0     ok
#> 4  1.5539111 1.6822352 12        0     ok
#> 5  0.3442215 0.5400380 11        0     ok
#> 6 -5.8298151 0.5859734 12        0     ok
head(JKpp(res_wle, cmeth = "AMT")$estimates)
#>     estimate        SE  L excluded status
#> 1 -0.3469704 0.6735435 12        0     ok
#> 2  1.3328207 0.6208916 12        0     ok
#> 3  1.0918816 0.4916653 12        0     ok
#> 4  2.0189363 1.6822352 12        0     ok
#> 5  0.7792898 0.5400380 11        0     ok
#> 6 -5.1186492 0.5859734 12        0     ok

Plausible values

Plausible values are draws from the posterior distribution of each person. They need a prior, so PV() takes an estimate of type "eap" or "map" and uses its prior (here different for women and men).

set.seed(1)
pv <- PV(res_eap, npv = 5)
head(pv$pvdraws)
#>             PV1        PV2        PV3        PV4        PV5
#> [1,] -0.8002389 -0.3233673 -0.9233717  0.5076070 -0.2375027
#> [2,]  0.4360231  1.2839471  1.4466054  1.3412268  0.7699550
#> [3,]  1.6063897  0.8976006  0.2588440 -0.7478307  1.3619954
#> [4,]  0.4252652  0.4445135  1.0874052  1.0052948  0.8530677
#> [5,]  0.8941050  0.8083111  0.3646916 -0.9293031  0.7065487
#> [6,] -2.0791640 -2.1387964 -2.9255585 -2.3316668 -1.7955193

By default (approx = TRUE) the values are drawn from a normal distribution with the posterior mean and standard deviation. With approx = FALSE they are drawn from the posterior itself.

References

Schuster, C., & Yuan, K. H. (2011). Robust estimation of latent ability in item response models. Journal of Educational and Behavioral Statistics, 36(6), 720–735.

Wainer, H., & Wright, B. D. (1980). Robust estimation of ability in the Rasch model. Psychometrika, 45(3), 373–391.

Warm, T. A. (1989). Weighted likelihood estimation of ability in item response theory. Psychometrika, 54, 427–450.
